title: The King's Heart in the LORD's Hand
summary: The chapter opens with the king's heart as a channel of water that the LORD directs wherever he pleases, and it closes with the reminder that no wisdom or plan prevails against the LORD and that victory belongs to him even when the war horse is ready. Between those frames it prizes justice above sacrifice, warns against haste, lying, pleasure, and greed, laments a contentious home, and contrasts the craving slacker with the righteous who give without holding back.
story: The collection has repeatedly set human plans under the LORD's rule (16:1, 9; 19:21; 20:24). Chapter 21 carries that theme to its highest human point, the king, and to its most dangerous human enterprise, war. If the heart of the most powerful man in the land is a stream the LORD directs (verse 1), and if the best-equipped army still depends on the LORD for victory (verse 31), then no one stands outside his rule. Between those frames the chapter returns to the everyday matters that fill the whole collection. The final section of the Solomonic proverbs (22:1-16) follows, and then a new collection begins.
historical:
Verse 31 reflects the military world of the ancient Near East, where horses were used mainly to pull war chariots and were costly symbols of power. The law warned Israel's king not to multiply horses for himself (Deuteronomy 17:16), yet Solomon built up a large chariot force and traded in horses from Egypt and Kue (1 Kings 10:26-29). The Psalms echo verse 31: some trust in chariots and some in horses, but Israel is to trust in the name of the LORD (Psalm 20:7). The saying does not forbid preparing for battle; it forbids trusting the preparation.

Verse 3 says that doing righteousness and justice pleases the LORD more than sacrifice. This is the language of the prophets and of Samuel's rebuke of Saul (1 Samuel 15:22; Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6-8). Proverbs does not reject the temple's worship, but it insists, like the prophets, that sacrifice cannot substitute for justice. Verse 27 sharpens the point: a sacrifice brought with evil intent is worse still, perhaps an attempt to buy God's favor for a wrong one plans to commit.
cultural:
Verse 1 uses the picture of irrigation channels. In Egypt and Mesopotamia, and in the gardens and orchards of Israel, farmers dug small channels from a water source and directed the flow by opening or blocking them, sometimes simply with a foot or a hoe (compare Deuteronomy 11:10). The water goes wherever the farmer turns it. So the LORD turns the king's heart, not by overriding it but as easily as a gardener guides water.

Verses 9 and 19 prefer a corner of the roof or the desert to life with a contentious wife. Israelite houses had flat roofs used for storage, drying crops, sleeping in hot weather, and sometimes a small upper room (2 Kings 4:10). Living on a corner of the roof meant exposure to sun and rain, and living in the desert meant exile from the community. The sayings are exaggerations that express how miserable a home without peace can be. Verse 9 is repeated in 25:24, and the same sentiment appears in 19:13 and 27:15.
literary: The chapter is framed by sayings about the LORD's sovereignty (verses 1-2 and 30-31), and several of its sayings name him or allude to him (verses 1, 2, 3, 12, 30, 31). Verse 12 speaks of the Righteous One, which many interpreters take as a title for God, though some think it refers to a righteous man observing the wicked. Verse 2 almost repeats 16:2, and verse 3 anticipates verse 27, both concerning sacrifice. Verses 9 and 19 are a matching pair of better-than sayings about domestic strife. Verses 25 and 26 form a unit on the slacker's endless craving contrasted with the righteous man's giving. Verse 4 is difficult in Hebrew; the word the BSB renders guides (nir) can mean lamp or a newly plowed field, and interpreters differ on the image. Verse 30's triple no, no wisdom, no understanding, no counsel, gives the closing verdict great force.

outline.t: The king's heart, the LORD who weighs hearts, and justice above sacrifice
Haste, lying fortunes, and the crooked way
A corner of the roof, the mocker punished, and the cry of the poor
Secret gifts, justice done, pleasure, and the desert
The treasures of the wise, guarding the tongue, and the craving slacker
Sacrifice with ill intent, false witness, and the LORD's victory

doctrines.note: The king's heart is a stream in the LORD's hand (verse 1), and no wisdom or counsel can prevail against him (verse 30). God's rule extends over the most powerful people and the most carefully prepared plans.

The LORD prefers righteousness and justice to sacrifice (verse 3), and a sacrifice brought with evil intent is detestable to him (verse 27). Worship cannot be separated from life, and God's holiness includes his demand for justice.
The one who shuts his ears to the cry of the poor will cry out and not be answered (verse 13). God's judgment often corresponds to the sin: the one who refused to hear finds himself unheard.

words.note: Peleg, channel or stream, especially an irrigation channel. The same word appears in Psalm 1:3 for the streams of water beside which the righteous are planted. In verse 1 it pictures the king's heart as water the LORD directs wherever he pleases, a vivid image of providence working through human decisions.

Mishpat, justice or judgment. The word covers a court's verdict, a legal right, and the broader order of fairness that God requires. It appears three times here: doing justice pleases the LORD more than sacrifice (verse 3), the wicked refuse to do what is just (verse 7), and justice done brings joy to the righteous and terror to evildoers (verse 15).

Nir, a lamp, or in a related form a freshly plowed field. The BSB renders it guides in verse 4, following the sense of a lamp that lights the way, so that haughty eyes and a proud heart are the lamp of the wicked. Others read it as the plowed field, the produce or harvest of the wicked. On either reading, what the wicked live by is sin.

christ: Verse 1's picture of the LORD turning a king's heart appears throughout Scripture, as in his turning of Cyrus to send the exiles home (Ezra 1:1). The New Testament's deepest example is the trial of Jesus, when Herod and Pilate, with the nations and the people of Israel, did what God's hand and plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:27-28). The rulers acted freely and wickedly, yet God directed their decisions toward redemption. Verse 3's preference for justice over sacrifice is one Jesus quoted in its prophetic form, twice citing Hosea's words about mercy rather than sacrifice (Matthew 9:13; 12:7). And verse 31's claim that victory belongs to the LORD is fulfilled in a way no war horse could achieve, in the cross and resurrection, where Paul says God gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 15:57). These are thematic links, not predictions in the proverbs themselves.

hard.q: What does verse 18 mean when it says the wicked become a ransom for the righteous?
hard.a:
The verse is puzzling because in the rest of Scripture a ransom is paid by one party to free another, and it is hard to see how the wicked could pay anything for the righteous. Most interpreters read it in light of 11:8, which says the righteous are delivered from trouble and the wicked go in their place. On this reading the saying describes a reversal: the disaster that threatened the righteous falls instead on the wicked, as when Haman was hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai (Esther 7:10). The word ransom is used loosely, for one taking the place of another in trouble.

Some readers see a broader principle: when God judges, the guilty bear the penalty they sought to bring on the innocent, which is the logic of the law of the false witness (Deuteronomy 19:19). Christian readers naturally notice the contrast with the gospel, where the righteous one gives his life as a ransom for the unrighteous (Mark 10:45; 1 Peter 3:18). That is not what the proverb means, but the reversal is striking: in Proverbs the wicked take the place of the righteous in judgment, while in the gospel the righteous takes the place of the wicked.

questions: Verse 1 says the king's heart is in the LORD's hand. How does that change the way you think about people in power whom you distrust?
Verse 3 says righteousness and justice please the LORD more than sacrifice. Where might religious practice be standing in for justice in your life?
Verse 31 says the horse is prepared for battle but victory is from the LORD. How do you work hard at your preparations without trusting in them?
